quarterly_data.signal: Q4 2025 results beat the high end of guidance: revenue $1.89 billion, down 5% sequentially and up 16% year on year (all end markets exceeded expectations, with the largest upside in communications on 'strong iOS demand'); gross margin 16.7%, which included a benefit of approximately $30 million from asset sales; operating income $185 million (9.8% margin); net income $172 million; EPS $0.69; EBITDA $369 million (19.5%). Q4 end markets year on year: communications +28% (stronger footprint in the current generation of iOS phones; communications 'stabilized with a key socket gain'), computing +6%, automotive & industrial +25% (advanced ADAS content; mainstream automotive posted a third consecutive quarter of sequential growth), consumer -10% (product life cycle of a high-volume wearable introduced in 2024). Full-year 2025: revenue grew 6% to $6.7 billion with every end market growing and RECORD computing revenue (+16% for the year, 'driven by strength in AI-related PC devices and networking infrastructure'); advanced packaging revenue set a new record, +7%; gross margin 14% including a 90 basis point headwind from the Vietnam ramp-up; operating income $467 million; EPS $1.50; EBITDA $1.16 billion; free cash flow $380 million. Year-end cash and short-term investments $2 billion, total liquidity $3 billion (+30%), total debt $1.4 billion, 1.2 times debt to EBITDA.
quarterly_data.figure: Q4 revenue $1.89 billion (-5% QoQ, +16% YoY), GM 16.7%, EPS $0.69; FY2025 revenue $6.7 billion (+6%)

quarterly_data.signal: Q1 2026 guidance given on this call: revenue between $1.6 billion and $1.7 billion, 'representing a 25% year-on-year increase at the midpoint' (CEO: $1.65 billion), with strong year-on-year growth in communications, computing and automotive & industrial; gross margin between 12.5% and 13.5%; operating expenses rising to approximately $135 million as R&D spend grows; net income $45 million to $70 million; EPS $0.18 to $0.28; FY2026 effective tax rate around 20%. CFO's margin bridge: the Q1 gross-margin step-down reflects the Q4 asset sale not repeating - without it the flow-through would 'pretty much be in line with our 30% model'; sequentially, favorable product mix is offset by incremental costs, and year over year there is 'material content impact as well as some potential currency headwinds'. For the full year management expects to achieve the 30% incremental flow-through (absent the one-time asset sale), helped by margin initiatives - 'optimization in Japan, Vietnam ramp-up efficiencies, a more favorable pricing environment, and a sustained mix shift towards high-value advanced packaging'. Equipment spending front-end loaded in 2026 'is going to put pressure on depreciation expense', with efficiencies expected as the second-half programs ramp.
quarterly_data.figure: Q1 2026 guide: revenue between $1.6 billion and $1.7 billion (25% YoY at midpoint), GM between 12.5% and 13.5%, EPS between $0.18 and $0.28

quarterly_data.signal: FY2026 outlook given on this call: revenue growth driven by computing, 'expected to grow over 20%', and continued strong growth in advanced automotive (ADAS, in-car computing, infotainment), while 'The remainder of our business is expected to grow in the single digits'. On technology, the CEO said 'when we look at the 2.5D and HDFO platforms, we're expecting that to nearly triple over the course of this year'. Asked for the AI-related advanced packaging share of revenue, he said Amkor 'exited '25 at about 20% of revenue' and will 'continue to see accelerated growth in that AI data center slash, you know, even PC area'. Within computing the PC market (units projected slightly down) is 'relatively soft compared to data center', though the shift to AI applications and more ARM-based designs benefits Amkor as the model moves from vertically integrated IDMs to outsourced/fabless. Other markets: phone units roughly flat with a premium-tier shift that favors Amkor's content; car units roughly flat, mainstream auto in a 'very slow recovery'. 2025 delivered record advanced and computing revenue 'driven by deep customer engagements across AI and HPC', and Amkor ramped its first high-density fan-out (HDFO) programs into high-volume production across multiple customers.
quarterly_data.figure: 2.5D + HDFO platforms expected to nearly triple in 2026; computing to grow over 20%; asked for the AI-related share, CEO: exited 2025 at about 20% of revenue

quarterly_data.signal: 2026 capex first guided on this call to rise to a range of $2.5 billion to $3 billion, from $905 million in 2025 (2025 came in below guidance because of the timing of Arizona cash payments, which shift into 2026): 65% to 70% for facility expansion including Phase One of the Arizona campus, about 30% to 35% for HDFO, test and other advanced packaging capacity, the remainder R&D and quality. Q&A detail: the equipment portion is 'not equipment for U.S. manufacturing' - it all supports Korea HDFO and test plus '300-millimeter capacity expansion in Taiwan' - and is 'about a 40% increase on equipment' year on year, which 'highlights the strong demand that we're seeing in this advanced packaging area'. Of the $7 billion Arizona plan, Phase One is about half, with construction about 60% of that; the building completes around the middle of 2027, so Phase One spend falls in 2026 and the first half of 2027, and the CFO said 'our Arizona investment most likely could peak in '26' because incentives arrive on a lag ('really minimal offsets' in the 2026 guide). Government incentives on the total project 'could be upwards of $2.85 billion'. Customer commitments (e.g. prepayment or loading agreements) also help fund the build - 'some that have already been executed and others that are in discussion' - and one HDFO CPU device ramping in 2026 'includes customer commitments to support our capacity investment'. Amkor says it can operate with $500 million of cash and expects interest expense to decrease even if debt rises, because construction interest is capitalized.
quarterly_data.figure: 2026 CapEx $2.5 billion to $3 billion (about a 40% increase on equipment); Arizona government incentives upwards of $2.85 billion

quarterly_data.signal: Asked about capacity to capture more computing demand, the CEO cited 'limitations' rather than hard constraints: (1) R&D/NPI bandwidth - the number of new product introductions customers want to run 'is creating some constraints where we're prioritizing larger opportunities specifically in Korea'; (2) floor space - SiP products are migrating from Korea to Vietnam to free Korean space for HDFO and test growth (flexibility 'until our Arizona facility comes online'), existing Korean building space was converted to clean room during 2025, and a new Korea building comes online as Amkor exits 2026, so 'we'll basically be increasing our Korea space around 20% since the beginning of '25'; (3) equipment delivery, front-end loaded in 2026 to support second-half launches. Vietnam reached breakeven in Q4 (after a 90 basis point 2025 gross-margin headwind) and is seen holding there in Q1, with no meaningful gross-margin impact going forward beyond SiP product mix. 2026 priorities: Arizona construction milestones, expanding advanced packaging capacity in Korea and Taiwan, and continuing to scale Vietnam.
quarterly_data.figure: Korea space up around 20% from the beginning of 2025 to exit 2026; Vietnam breakeven in Q4

quarterly_data.signal: Data-center HDFO pipeline as of this call: 'We have two additional programs in final qualification for HDFO supporting AI data centers, in addition to the two HDFO PC devices we've discussed previously', and the Korea team is preparing to launch both into high volume in the second half of 2026. Both data-center programs are 'CPU-related'; the customers are existing Amkor customers, but 'one of them is new to the HDFO platform'. One of the HDFO CPU devices ramping this year 'includes customer commitments to support our capacity investment'. Ramp shape: one of the two devices is expected to be 'in very high volume. It'll be a pretty steep ramp', while the other is ramping but it is hard to project whether it reaches full volume by year-end - 'definitely meaningful revenue contribution'. PC-related HDFO products ramp earlier in the year (one already in production), then 'there'll be a pretty sizable step up in the CPU data center type devices' in the second half, making the revenue growth 'back-end second half loaded'. Computing (PC plus data center) is expected to grow over 20% in 2026, with PC relatively soft versus data center, and the majority of 2026 equipment investment is focused on HDFO and test.
quarterly_data.figure: two data-center HDFO CPU programs in final qualification for high volume in the second half of 2026; computing to grow over 20%

quarterly_data.signal: TSMC partnership status on this call: asked (by an analyst citing reported TSMC shortages) how the Arizona partnership with TSMC is progressing, the CEO said 'U.S. manufacturing is still a couple of years away', so today's constraints are being supported 'out of our Korea facility. Little bit out of Taiwan as well'. On TSMC: 'I'd say that discussion continues. We have a very strong ongoing relationship on technology. As well as what type of manufacturing is going to be needed in the U.S.', a collaboration that 'spirals down to end customers that are going to ultimately benefit from that U.S. supply chain'. Customer interest in US packaging 'is continuing to increase' - the October Arizona groundbreaking was attended by many customers across communications, automotive and consumer. Arizona Phase One construction is underway, with the building completing around the middle of 2027.

players.product: OSAT assembly/test and supplemental advanced packaging

quarterly_data.signal: Early read on memory supply at the OSAT level: 'We continue to monitor export control and trade policies as well as dynamics around substrates, advanced silicon, and memory supply. We have considered these items in our guidance for Q1.' Asked about Android weakness (an analyst cited Qualcomm's guidance), the CEO said for Q1 'maybe this is related to memory and other things' - Android shows 'maybe a little bit of a step down. But in general, nothing that's concerning for us', which he said 'could be related to the shift to more premium where we participate a little more heavily', while iOS is exiting 'a pretty solid' phone-launch cycle. Market data project phone units roughly flat.
